summary: A note on socket number assignment. It warns of the danger of imposing more fixed socket number requirements on hosts and relates to RFCs 542, 503 and 451.

plainLanguage.summary: Giving every service a fixed spot number gets crowded and rigid. The author asks not to hand out more fixed numbers.

subtitle: Why protocols should not require fixed socket numbers

tldr.problem: Some network protocols were starting to require specific socket numbers relative to other sockets, which created implementation difficulties on different host systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 617 argues that the Host-Host Protocol leaves socket number assignment to the host, and that protocols should negotiate dynamically rather than imposing fixed numbers, except for initial connection setup.
tldr.outcome: The RFC advocates for negotiation over Telnet connections to establish data channels instead of relying on fixed socket offsets.

today: RFC 617 is a protocol design note that helped establish principles for how network protocols should handle resource allocation and negotiation, rather than making rigid assumptions about host systems.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Some protocols were making assumptions about socket number assignment. For example, the File Transfer Protocol (RFC 542) assumed that data transfer sockets would be at specific offsets from the initial connection socket. This created problems because different host systems had different ways of managing socket numbers.

The author, Edward Taft, explains that such fixed requirements did not account for the flexibility different operating systems need in their socket number allocation strategies.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers assign mailbox numbers in different ways. Asking for a specific number sometimes doesn't work.

sections.title: Socket Number Assignment Methods
sections.content:
The RFC describes how the Harvard NCP implementation on PDP-10 systems allowed programs to specify socket numbers in multiple ways: as job-relative, user-relative, or guaranteed unique numbers assigned by the system itself. This flexibility made fixed socket requirements incompatible with the architecture.

When protocols like FTP demanded that data connections use specific socket offsets, server implementations that separated control and data functions into different processes could not meet these requirements without complex workarounds.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems let you say 'use a number near this one,' others let you pick a number yourself, and others have the system pick for you. Asking for a specific number breaks some of these systems.

sections.title: Recommended Approach
sections.content:
RFC 617 recommends that only the initial connection (ICP) should use reserved socket numbers. For any additional connections needed, protocols should exchange socket numbers through negotiation over the existing Telnet connection, in the form of messages like 'Please connect to my socket xxxxxx'.

This approach avoids making unwarranted assumptions about how individual host systems assign and manage socket numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying 'use socket number 500,' programs should ask 'connect to whatever socket I tell you to use.'

references.text: Abhay, K., et al., "File Transfer Protocol", RFC 542, July 1973.
Krilanovich, M., "Socket Number List", RFC 503, May 1973.
Padlipsky, M., "ICP: A proposed uniform approach to Interprocess Communication in the ARPA Computer Network", RFC 501, May 1973.
